Issued at 323 AM EDT Thu Oct 8 2026

=== Warm and Dry Through Friday ===

A weakening cold front is pushing through the region this morning 
and is currently located over central Kentucky. The front is 
expected to exit southern Kentucky around sunrise. A few mid-level 
clouds and a sharp northerly wind shift are noted along the cold 
front. The name "cold" front is a little misleading, as we will not 
see a change in temperatures. Though, this front will reinforce the 
dry airmass and keep quiet conditions through Friday. 

During the afternoon, we will see peak mixing up to about 825mb. 
This will help to bring drier air down to the surface and for high 
temperatures to overachieve. HREF probabilities show a 50% chance of 
dew points less than 40F this afternoon. Temperatures will be in the 
upper 70s in the Bluegrass and low 80s elsewhere. This will place 
afternoon RHs in the 20-25% range.

On Friday, winds will veer to the southeast as high pressure pushes 
off to the east and the tropical system approaches the Gulf states. 
Aloft, heights will increase as ridging shifts east and amplifies 
over the region. Expecting to see continued quiet, dry, and warm 
conditions. Afternoon RH will dip into the 22-28% range and 
temperatures will warm into the low-mid 80s. 

=== Remnants of Hurricane Isaias To Bring Rainfall This Weekend ===

The National Hurricane Center has classified Hurricane Isaias as a 
Category One Hurricane as of this writing. This storm is expected to 
intensify as it moves north through the northern Gulf and make 
landfall on the northern Gulf coast. This storm is currently 
expected to reach a peak intensity of a high-end Category 2 
Hurricane just prior to landfall Friday evening. Over the last 24 
hours, the track has shifted slightly east and has sped up. 

As the system moves north on Saturday, the rain shield will become 
expansive as it is quickly picked up by synoptic troughing. 
Currently, LREF cluster analysis and other ensembles show rain 
chances entering southern Kentucky and working north Saturday 
afternoon. Though, the gusty winds and better tropical rainfall will 
not enter southern Kentucky until Saturday evening and into the 
overnight hours. 

Given that this system is moving through at an instability minimum, 
this will luckily bring a very low chance for tropical tornadoes. 
Additionally, ensembles show low CAPE values, which increases 
confidence. Though, if this system does speed up, southern Kentucky 
may see a chance for tropical tornadoes in the evening. These 
tornadoes are weak and brief. 

Saturday evening and into the overnight hours, 850mb winds will be 
around 60-65kts and will quickly weaken. A stable layer at the 
surface will prevent any mixing of these winds down to the surface. 
Therefore, wind gusts are expected to be around 25-35mph over 
southern Kentucky and up to 25mph elsewhere. 

Given the strong LLJ in the northeastern portion of the tropical 
cyclone, areas in southern and central Kentucky will see beneficial 
rainfall on Saturday night and Sunday. Area-wide, QPF will range 
0.75-1.5 inches. Areas in southern and central KY may see totals up 
to 3 inches. Given very dry antecedent conditions, this rain is 
welcomed to help combat drought conditions. Any flooding concerns 
should remain localized during this event.

=== Drier Early Next Week ===

The remnant energy of the tropical cyclone will be swept northeast 
as troughing swings through the region. Precip chances will decrease 
from west to east early Monday morning. High pressure and ridging 
will build in behind, allowing for drier conditions and clearing 
skies. Temperatures look to remain slightly above normal in the 
upper 70s and low 80s through Tuesday. Mid week, stronger troughing 
may move across the northern CONUS and bring a cold front through 
the Ohio Valley.
